source: Holyoak & Thagard (1997) The analogical mind
finding: States the multiconstraint theory: analogy is guided by three soft pressures, similarity, structure (isomorphism: consistent one-to-one correspondences) and purpose (the reasoner's goal). They act like forces in design, not rigid rules, and are resolved by constraint satisfaction.
numbers: Three constraint classes. Worked example is a 24-month-old child (Aaron) mapping a kissed injury onto his mother's injury. Structure beat object similarity (mother not mapped to herself).
quote: These three kinds of constraints--similarity, structure, and purpose--do not operate like rigid rules
limits: Narrative anecdote plus lab review; no new data in the theory statement itself. The relative weights of the constraints are not fixed by the theory.
agent_relevance: The agent's choice among candidate mappings should score each candidate on three separate axes (feature overlap, relational consistency, goal relevance), not on one similarity number.

source: Holyoak & Thagard (1989) Analogical mapping by constraint satisfaction
finding: Defines ACME. Each possible pairing of a source and a target element becomes a mapping unit in a localist network. Excitatory links join pairings that support each other (same proposition, consistent arguments). Inhibitory links join pairings that compete (same element mapped twice). A semantic unit pushes up similar pairings. A pragmatic unit pushes up IMPORTANT elements and PRESUMED pairings. Activation is updated by the Grossberg (1978) rule.
numbers: Defaults in all reported runs: decay d=.1, excitation e=.1, inhibition i=-.2, min=-1, max=1, p1=.1 (IMPORTANT), p2=.3 (PRESUMED). Units start at .01. Similarity weight .1 for identical predicates. Network typically settles in well under 100 cycles; never over 220.
limits: Hand-built predicate-calculus inputs; results depend on the representation the authors chose. Semantic and pragmatic weights are set by hand.
agent_relevance: A cheap, explicit scoring scheme exists: enumerate hypothesis pairs, add support and conflict links, relax. Code can pick among rival mappings this way, with the model only supplying the propositions.

source: Holyoak & Thagard (1989) Analogical mapping by constraint satisfaction
finding: ACME sensitivity analysis. It works over a wide parameter range. Excitation above .12 becomes unstable. High inhibition can block recovery from an early wrong mapping. Inhibition should exceed excitation to separate best from second-best units.
numbers: Decay .001 to .2 works equally well. Excitation .01 to .12 works for all examples. Inhibition up to -.9 tolerated. p2 for PRESUMED works best near .3. Authors report no case where a correct mapping was overtaken after it led.
limits: Tested mainly on the laser/radiation and water/heat-flow examples. The ARCS paper uses different defaults (e=.01, d=.04, i=-.04), so values are model-specific.
agent_relevance: Winner-take-all selection has a known risk: a sticky first guess. This fits guardrail G1 (doubt only on a signal) and the need for a check before committing.

source: Holyoak & Thagard (1989) Analogical mapping by constraint satisfaction
finding: ACME simulates Holyoak & Koh (1987) convergence-problem analogies. It finds the correct mapping in all four lightbulb versions. Surface similarity (laser vs ultrasound) has no measurable effect on mapping difficulty. In the poor-constraint versions the key proposition (do not destroy healthy tissue) has no mapping at all, offered as the reason transfer failed for people.
numbers: Table 5 as extracted (column order garbled in the scan): cycles to success 3, 38, 5, 5 across the four versions. Human convergence solutions before a hint: 69%, 38%, 33%, 13%. After a hint: 75%, 81%, 60%, 47% (row-to-version pairing uncertain). Table 4: network settled by cycle 31, goodness 4.84.
limits: The scan's table layout is scrambled, so which cycle count belongs to which version is uncertain. Mapping only; retrieval is left to ARCS.
agent_relevance: Mapping failure and retrieval failure differ. Once a source is in hand, structure carries the day over surface; before that, surface cues dominate. Do not use one similarity test for both finding and mapping analogs.

source: Holyoak & Thagard (1989) Analogical mapping by constraint satisfaction
finding: ACME on the Gentner & Toupin 'jealous animal' stories. Systematicity matters only when similarity misleads. In the cross-mapped condition ACME fails to find the right mapping if the stories are unsystematic. It succeeds if inhibition i is reduced from -.2 to -.1 or min is raised from -1 to -.3.
numbers: Table 15 cycles to success (as extracted, order uncertain): systematic 3, 4, 38; unsystematic 3, 4, no success. Similarity weight .06 for similar characters, .01 for dissimilar, .1 for identical predicates.
limits: ACME shows smaller differences between the same-object and different-object conditions than the human data did (authors say so). The cross-mapped fix was parameter tuning after the fact.
agent_relevance: Shows the central failure mode: when object similarity points the wrong way, only strong relational structure rescues the right mapping. Code should flag cross-mapped cases (similar objects in different roles) as the dangerous ones.

source: Holyoak & Thagard (1989) Analogical mapping by constraint satisfaction
finding: Comparison with SME (Falkenhainer, Forbus, Gentner). ACME treats isomorphism, semantic similarity and pragmatic centrality as parallel pressures that give one best mapping. SME builds consistent subsets of identical relations first and ranks them. ACME can map predicates that share only argument count; SME needs identical relations. ACME uses systematicity symmetrically, as a special case of interrelated propositions.
numbers: Boys-dogs problem (three boys with three unary predicates, three dogs with different predicates): ACME finds the unique isomorphism with no semantic help.
quote: ACME can be characterized as an extension of SME, even though it operates differently.
limits: The comparison is the authors' own 1989 reading of SME. LISA's authors later argue ACME is too powerful on such unnatural problems.
agent_relevance: The real split is soft joint weighing (ACME) vs a hard structural filter first (SME). The hard filter is cheap and checkable in code; the soft weighing handles ambiguity.

source: Holyoak & Thagard (1989) Analogical mapping by constraint satisfaction
finding: ACME's Socrates-as-midwife metaphor runs show pragmatic and structural support interacting. Non-isomorphic versions settle more slowly and some elements get no mapping.
numbers: Cycles to settle for three versions: 34 (isomorphic, nonpragmatic), 105 (nonisomorphic, nonpragmatic), 83 (nonisomorphic, pragmatic). Pragmatic support shortens settling by 22 cycles in the non-isomorphic case.
limits: Single worked example; numbers come from the model, not from human data.
agent_relevance: A goal signal reduces the work needed to resolve a messy mapping. This supports passing the task goal into the mapping step.

source: Holyoak & Thagard (1997) The analogical mind
finding: Spellman & Holyoak (1992) Persian Gulf study as reviewed. Undergraduates mapping the 1991 Gulf War onto World War II gave a bistable mapping. Either US-1991 = US-WW2, Bush = FDR, Saudi Arabia = Britain; or US-1991 = Britain, Bush = Churchill, Saudi Arabia = France. One-to-one and consistency kept leaders and countries together. Kuwait mapped to Austria or Poland either way.
numbers: Run in the first two days of the January 1991 counterattack. A second group could be steered to either pattern by reading a slightly biased but accurate WW2 summary (emphasising Churchill/Britain or Roosevelt/US). Exact percentages are not given in the 1997 review.
limits: Original percentages are in the 1992 paper, which was not opened. Mapping answers were written, not timed.
agent_relevance: Rival global mappings can both be coherent. The agent should keep the second-best coherent mapping alive as an alternative, not blend the two.

source: Spellman & Holyoak (1996) Pragmatics in analogical mapping
finding: Experiment 1: processing goals reverse the mapping of an ambiguous element. Participants judged countries on trade or on membership before mapping. The ambiguous country Anthar went to prosperous Grandus under a trade goal and to benevolent Minutus under a membership goal.
numbers: Trade: 54% Grandus vs 19% Minutus. Membership: 21% Grandus vs 58% Minutus. chi2(1,N=53)=11.78, p<.001. 116 recruited, 12 dropped, 104 analysed. 78 of 100 mapped the President to the King.
limits: Student sample, science-fiction countries, written mappings. The goal was manipulated by an orienting task before mapping.
agent_relevance: Direct support for purpose as a real constraint inside mapping: changing the stated goal changes which mapping wins. The task goal text should enter mapping selection.

source: Spellman & Holyoak (1996) Pragmatics in analogical mapping
finding: Experiment 2 separates relation-focus from object-focus manipulations and shows goal-irrelevant information still enters the mapping (attenuation, not a hard filter). For the ambiguous country Barebrute, mappings followed the encouraged alternative. Mapping from the 4-country planet to the 3-country planet, many participants mapped both rivals onto Barebrute.
numbers: Collapsed analysis chi2(1,N=108)=8.85, p<.01. 159 analysed of 165. Control condition: 8 of 16 (50%) gave the many-to-one mapping. Across the four goal conditions 32% did. About 90% mapped the unambiguous countries as expected (Afflu-Grainwell, Compak-Mightless). Relation vs object manipulations did not differ.
limits: Many-to-one answers might reflect an answer format that allowed several entries; the authors note this.
agent_relevance: The goal re-weights other constraints but does not delete them. A scaffold that drops all goal-irrelevant structure once a goal is set would lose information the human mind keeps.

source: Spellman & Holyoak (1996) Pragmatics in analogical mapping
finding: Experiment 3 (soap-opera plagiarism, Austin undergraduates) shows all three constraints at once in a four-way ambiguous mapping. The goal-relevant relation (professional or romantic) dominated, and the incidental inheritance relation also mattered, more in the explicit mapping task than in the plot-extension task.
numbers: N=128. Plot task: 88% wrote an analogous continuation; 97% of those matched the focus; analysed n=107, chi2=95.33. Mapping task (n=88 with congruous Peter/Mary pairs): 72% goal-consistent vs 28%, chi2=16.41; 65% followed the incidental inheritance relation vs 35%, chi2=7.68, p<.01; Professional beat Romantic 65% vs 35%. 23 vs 1 participants were goal-consistent in the plot task but not the mapping task, chi2(1,N=24)=20.17.
limits: 31% of the mapping-task group were dropped for non-congruous Peter/Mary mappings. Explicit mapping weakens the goal effect by design.
agent_relevance: Structure (a consistent Peter/Mary pair), similarity (like relations to like) and purpose act together. Asking for an explicit mapping lets more constraints in than asking for an inference, so the scaffold may want both views.

source: Spellman & Holyoak (1996) Pragmatics in analogical mapping
finding: ACME reproduces the goal-driven reversals when goals are implemented as selective attention (inhibitory weighting of goal-irrelevant propositions). It fits Experiment 1 (the Anthar reversal), Experiment 2 and the earlier Experiment 3*.
numbers: Experiment 2 network: 46 source propositions, 49 target propositions, 1,207 mapping units, 22,271 links, five runs (Military, Economic, Millpower, Hungerall, Control). Only ordinal agreement with human data is claimed.
limits: No quantitative fit. Hand-built representations.
agent_relevance: Goal as an attention filter that scales which relations count, not as a new rule, is a workable design.

source: Thagard, Holyoak, Nelson & Gochfeld (1990) Analog retrieval by constraint satisfaction (ARCS)
finding: ARCS applies the same three constraints to retrieval. A probe links only to stored structures with semantically similar predicates, then structure and pragmatic support settle in a network. It reproduces the ordering of Holyoak & Koh (1987) retrievability.
numbers: Tumor probe against 5 radiation problems: 100 units, 1,104 links, 95 cycles. Human spontaneous convergence solutions vs ARCS activation: laser/fragile 69% vs .22; ultrasound/fragile 38% vs .15; laser/insufficient 33% vs .11; ultrasound/insufficient 13% vs .05; fortress about 30% vs -.12 (mismatch blamed on different subjects and memory competition).
limits: Fortress data came from other experiments and subjects. Defaults e=.01, d=.04, i=-.04. Semantic overlap acts as a gate: structure alone cannot retrieve a far analog.
agent_relevance: Retrieval of far analogs is the weak step for people and for ARCS. Expect cross-domain sources to need an explicit prompt or a generated abstract description, not spontaneous recall.

source: Thagard, Holyoak, Nelson & Gochfeld (1990) Analog retrieval by constraint satisfaction (ARCS)
finding: ARCS scaling and robustness tests. A fables database (100 Aesop fables, about 22 propositions each) and a plays database (24 Shakespeare synopses, about 55 propositions each). Links grow about as the square of database size; units grow linearly. Hamlet retrieved six tragedies. A West Side Story outline retrieved Romeo and Juliet.
numbers: Plays: Hamlet probe against 23 plays gave 1,160 units, 67,140 links, 268 cycles. Fables: 10 random probes into databases of 10 to 99 fables. Deleting 25% of units broke the fit to human data 75% of the time; deleting 10% of concepts broke it 60% of the time. Excitation above .0145 gave oscillation.
limits: Fragile to damage, unlike the usual graceful-degradation claim. Representations were hand-written.
agent_relevance: Pairwise link cost grows fast (quadratic). A code-side retrieval stage should prune by predicate overlap first, as ARCS does, before any joint settling.

source: Krawczyk, Holyoak & Hummel (2004) Structural constraints and object similarity in analogical mapping and inference
finding: Under high relational complexity, object similarity and relational structure carry equal weight in both mapping and inference. This contradicts the view that relational structure dominates. LISA, which treats both as soft constraints in a limited working memory, reproduced it. SME, which puts structure first, did not.
numbers: N=48 UCLA students. Mean 2.36 mappings per character. Mapping proportions: object-similar O=.33, relational R=.30, mixed SO=.32, unrelated U=.06 (F(3,141)=21.64, p<.01). Inferences: O=.28, R=.23, SO=.50, U=.02 (F(3,141)=18.78). Rank-1 plausibility: O=.33, R=.23, others=.04 (F(2,94)=6.65). LISA over 50 runs: O inference 24%, R inference 18%, mixtures 48%.
limits: One story pair; participants could write several mappings per character. Participants' own reasons named trait information as a strong basis.
agent_relevance: Even when a clean relational answer exists, people pick the object-similar answer about as often. Check agent output for object-similarity capture when roles are crossed.

source: Hummel & Holyoak (1997) Distributed representations of structure: a theory of analogical access and mapping (LISA)
finding: LISA recasts the multiconstraint theory in a symbolic-connectionist model with limited working memory and synchrony binding. It lists 14 empirical phenomena an analogy model must cover, including semantic similarity weighing more in access than in mapping, isomorphism weighing more in mapping, and pragmatic centrality.
numbers: Simulated Ross (1989) access/mapping dissociations (means of 3 runs), Barebrute weights (7 conditions) and the soap-opera Experiment 3 (four focus levels, two orders each). Boys-dogs problem: LISA succeeded only when all 10 propositions of both analogs were in the phase set together, beyond human working-memory capacity.
limits: Qualitative fits only; the authors did not attempt a quantitative match. Phenomena 11 and 12 rest on informal observation.
agent_relevance: Working-memory limits on how many propositions are compared at once explain why unnatural mappings are hard. Chunk the comparison for the agent instead of dumping both analogs in at once.

source: Hummel & Holyoak (1997) Distributed representations of structure: a theory of analogical access and mapping (LISA)
finding: Ross (1989) shows that story-line similarity and similarity of objects in matching roles affect access and mapping differently. With similar story lines, similar objects in dissimilar roles hurt both. With dissimilar story lines they hurt mapping but little or not access. LISA reproduces these ordinal patterns.
numbers: Conditions coded {+,0}/{+,0,-}: story-line similarity / role-match similarity. Four ordinal comparisons per measure; LISA values are means of 3 runs. In convergence-problem studies, with a hint over 80% give the convergence solution whether the source is a close analog, far analog or schema.
limits: Ross data are second-hand from the LISA paper (Ross 1989 not opened). Ordinal fit only.
agent_relevance: Object similarity in crossed roles is a systematic trap that harms mapping even when it does not harm retrieval.

source: Wikipedia: Analogical reasoning (multiconstraint theory section)
finding: Summary: coherence depends on structural consistency, semantic similarity and purpose. The highest structural consistency is an isomorphism. The highest similarity is identical relations with many identical attributes. The theory has trouble with multiple sources. Hummel & Holyoak (2005) moved it into a neural network; Doumas, Hummel & Sandhofer (2008) learn relations from unstructured examples.
numbers: No numeric values in the section.
limits: Secondary source; used only to confirm the framing in the SUBFIELDS row.
agent_relevance: Names the open problem for the agent: how to combine several sources into one mapping.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) matched or beat UCLA undergraduates on text matrix reasoning, letter-string and verbal analogies, but was clearly worse on story analogies, especially far (cross-domain) ones.
numbers: Digit Matrices (N=40 humans): GPT-3 odds ratio vs humans 1.88 (p=.005) for generation, 6.27 (p=2.3e-8) for multiple choice. Story analogies (Gentner et al. materials, 18 source stories, N=54 humans): GPT-3 chose the causally matching story above chance in the near condition (binomial p=.0039) but not the far condition (p=.065); humans t(53)=16.7, p<1e-22. Overall human vs GPT-3 OR=0.37, p=.0003; 15 of 54 humans were right on every trial. GPT-4 was nearly perfect on near and better on far.
limits: Tests limited to a local context window. The story set is public and may have leaked into training; Lewis & Mitchell probe this.
agent_relevance: Cross-domain story mapping is the least reliable LLM analogy skill, which is where relational structure must beat surface. A code-side structure check would add the most value here.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models (supplement: Gick & Holyoak radiation paradigm)
finding: Qualitative replication of the Gick & Holyoak transfer paradigm. Alone, the radiation problem got a non-convergence answer (inject a source into the tumor). With a laser or ultrasound lightbulb story first, GPT-3 produced the convergence solution, even with the lower-surface-similarity ultrasound version. With two distracting stories added it lost the solution, and regained it when prompted to consider the earlier stories.
numbers: Single qualitative runs (Supplement S5.1 to S5.4); no counts.
limits: Anecdotal, not a rate. Whether the model had seen the radiation problem is unknown.
agent_relevance: The model shows the human spontaneous-retrieval failure and the human fix, an explicit instruction to check earlier material. Prompted retrieval is an operator to schedule only after a signal.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Evaluating the robustness of analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Re-tests Webb et al. with variants. On far-analogy story problems GPT-4 shows a large answer-order bias and drops more than humans when the correct story is paraphrased to remove sentence-level resemblance to the source. Part of the earlier LLM success may be surface similarity.
numbers: Original Webb et al. data for GPT-4: 0.89 (16/18) when the correct answer is first, 0.61 (11/18) when second, 0.75 overall. Their GPT-4: 1.0, 0.72, 0.86 (31/36). Humans (245 Prolific, 5 rejected): 0.78 either order (564/720). Paraphrased: GPT-4 0.86 to 0.72 (26/36); humans also fell.
limits: Only 18 stories; the authors say the paraphrase effect is hard to test for significance. Letter-string and matrix variants also collapse for GPT models on simple problems.
agent_relevance: Do not trust one run's pick between two candidate mappings. Swap candidate order and require agreement. Order bias is a G5 issue.

source: Sourati, Ilievski, Sommerauer & Jiang (2024) ARN: Analogical reasoning on narratives
finding: A benchmark that crosses surface mappings with system (relational) mappings in narratives, near and far. LLMs recognise near analogies but fail far ones, and cannot prefer a far analogy over a surface-similar distractor even when told to look for system mappings.
numbers: Zero-shot, chance 50%. Near analogies: models 75.0% vs humans 97.9%; SBERT 77.9%. Far analogies: models 39.6% (below chance) vs humans 94.1%. Near analogy vs far disanalogy 76.9%; (near,near) 73.2%; (far,far) 45.3%; far analogy vs near distractor 33.9%. GPT-4 best at 68.1% mean; SBERT 42.3%, and 1% on the far-vs-near case.
limits: Models: Llama 2, Flan-T5, UnifiedQA, GPT-3.5, GPT-4. Few-shot demonstrations at first reduced near-analogy skill; chain of thought helped somewhat.
agent_relevance: This is the multiconstraint conflict test, surface vs structure, and LLMs side with surface. It argues for external structure checking when sources are cross-domain.

source: Lee, Song, Yoon, Park & Kang (2025) The curious case of analogies: investigating analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Mechanistic study on proportional and story analogies. Relational information is encoded in middle-upper layers when the model is right. Failures also include not applying the relation to new entities, not only missing relations. Patching hidden states at key tokens recovers part of the failures. Linear probes separate analogical structure from lexical similarity in middle layers.
numbers: Patching gains of up to 38.4% of incorrect cases by replacing the first pair; up to 38.1% by patching a second-entity state to the link (Table 1: +32.3% / +25.9% rows for the experiments). Probe accuracy peaks in mid layers (figure; no single number extracted).
limits: Open-weight models only. Patching is a probe, not a fix usable in a prompt-only scaffold.
agent_relevance: Internal structure exists but is not reliably applied. Scaffold steps that make the mapping explicit (list the pairs, then apply them) address the right gap.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners
finding: Analogical prompting has the model write its own relevant examples and knowledge before solving. It beats 0-shot CoT and often manual few-shot CoT on GSM8K, MATH, Codeforces and BIG-Bench.
numbers: Codeforces Acc@1 (GPT3.5-turbo-16k): 0-shot 8%, 0-shot CoT 9%, 3-shot CoT 11%, self-generated exemplars 13%, self-generated knowledge plus exemplars 15% (Acc@10: 24, 27, 27, 25, 29). The GSM8K and MATH table columns were not cleanly extractable, so those gains are not quoted.
limits: This generates sources; it does not test choosing among mappings. Self-generated examples come from one model, so errors are correlated (G4).
agent_relevance: Self-generated analogs are cheap but come from the same model. Use them as candidate sources, then judge fit by code-checked structure and a real test, not by the model.

source: Hu, Storks, Lewis & Chai (2023) In-context analogical reasoning with pre-trained language models
finding: Pre-trained language models solve RAVEN matrix problems zero-shot once perceptual features are written as language. Higher abstraction (naming, then decomposing attributes) helps. Adding a distracting orientation attribute barely hurts.
numbers: GPT-3 175B Center sub-task: 77.2% with attribute naming, 80.0% with decomposition. Decomposition adds 2.8% for the largest model. Accuracy rises as matrix rows are added (in-context learning). Chance is 12.5%.
limits: Visual puzzle, not natural-language analogy. The abstraction was hand-designed.
agent_relevance: Re-encoding a problem into explicit relational language raises accuracy. This favours an explicit structure-writing step.

source: Liu, Dubova, Conklin, Harada & Griffiths (2026) Assessing the effect of cross-domain mapping on creativity in humans and large language models
finding: Random cross-domain source prompts raised originality for humans but gave LLMs no overall benefit. Only the best LLMs gained, and only when the source was far in semantic space. Humans transferred surface features; LLMs transferred structural and functional properties.
numbers: Humans N=140 (Prolific), 10 design challenges each; 2,800 rephrased ideas rated by judges; seven LLMs. Originality and feasibility trade off (r=-0.74). Cross-domain condition: o3 mean originality 3.83, Claude-Sonnet-4 3.76 (CI 3.61 to 3.91). Human user-need mean 2.57.
limits: Product design rated for originality, not mapping accuracy. Rephrasing used one LLM.
agent_relevance: The opposite human/LLM bias to the story studies: LLMs may favour structure when generating but surface when judging. Test the mapping step in both directions.

source: Holyoak & Koh (1987) Surface and structural similarity in analogical transfer (cited from ARCS and Webb et al.)
finding: Source of the four lightbulb/radiation versions that cross surface similarity (laser vs ultrasound) with structural constraint (fragile glass vs insufficient intensity). Both factors affected spontaneous transfer.
numbers: Quoted second-hand: 69%, 38%, 33%, 13% spontaneous convergence solutions; 75%, 81%, 60%, 47% after a hint (ARCS Table 2 and ACME Table 5).
limits: Not opened. Row pairing is partly garbled in the scans.
agent_relevance: The founding surface-by-structure 2x2 design; reuse it as a test on the agent.

source: Spellman & Holyoak (1992) If Saddam is Hitler then who is George Bush? Analogical mapping between systems of social roles
finding: First demonstration of bistable, internally consistent social-role mappings and of knowledge-guided choice between them (Persian Gulf vs WW2).
numbers: Quoted via Holyoak & Thagard (1997); exact percentages not available here.
limits: Not opened. Tied to January 1991 beliefs; many students knew little of WW2.
agent_relevance: Supports keeping two global mappings and ranking them rather than blending.

source: Falkenhainer, Forbus & Gentner (1989) The structure-mapping engine: algorithm and examples
finding: Rival model. Builds match hypotheses, forms structurally consistent global mappings, ranks them by systematicity. Pragmatics and semantics are kept outside the mapping stage.
numbers: None extracted. Krawczyk et al. (2004) report SME did not reproduce the equal weight on object and relational constraints.
limits: Not opened. Description comes from Holyoak & Thagard (1989) and Krawczyk et al. (2004).
agent_relevance: A code-side structural filter in the SME style is the checkable baseline. Multiconstraint scoring would be the ranker on top.

source: Doumas, Hummel & Sandhofer (2008) A theory of the discovery and predication of relational concepts (known via Wikipedia)
finding: Extends the LISA line to learn relations from unstructured examples, closing the gap of where relational representations come from.
numbers: None extracted.
limits: Not opened; known only from the Wikipedia summary.
agent_relevance: What the agent maps depends on the relational descriptions it first produces. The quality of that step bounds the whole mapping.
